courses.title: CARSI Trauma & Biohazard Decontamination Practitioner
courses.description:
An Australian- and New Zealand-produced credential course for restoration technicians, supervisors and support staff who decontaminate sites affected by blood and other body fluids after an injury, a death, an assault or a similar event. It builds safe, discreet field judgement. It is no substitute for an employer’s procedures, a product label and Safety Data Sheet, medical advice after an exposure, or the instructions of police, a coroner or a regulator.

Six modules follow the order of a real job: the work, the duty (Australian WHS, Victorian OHS and New Zealand HSWA) and conduct on site; blood-borne viruses, hepatitis B vaccination under the Australian and New Zealand Immunisation Handbooks, and the exposure response; site risk assessment, the SWMS and PPE; zones, containment, removal and the clean-then-disinfect sequence with TGA and ARTG claims checks in Australia and EPA NZ checks in New Zealand; sharps and clinical waste under state EPA and NZ council rules; and psychosocial hazards, verification and the defensible job file. Each module ends with a check. A practical task and a final designation exam complete the course.

CARSI Trauma & Biohazard Decontamination Practitioner is a CARSI Southern Hemisphere Restoration Designation. Standards are referenced by name only (aligned to the principles in ANSI/IICRC S540:2023). No standard text is reproduced.
courses.shortDescription: An Australian- and New Zealand-produced credential course leading to the CARSI Trauma & Biohazard Decontamination Practitioner designation: blood-borne virus safety, hepatitis B vaccination, risk assessment and PPE, clean-then-disinfect, sharps and clinical waste, and crew psychological safety.

modules.title: Module 1: The Work, the Duty and How This Course Works

lessons.title: What this course covers and who it is for
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Scenario and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

Your phone rings on a Sunday afternoon. A property manager in Parramatta needs a unit cleaned after a resident was found deceased. The family is distressed, the neighbours are watching, and the manager wants to know when it will be “back to normal”. Across the Tasman, a café owner in Christchurch calls about an injury in the kitchen that left blood on a vinyl floor and a timber bench. Both calls need the same thing from you: a calm, careful professional who protects themselves, their crew, the client and the people grieving, and who leaves the site safe and properly documented.

The idea

Trauma and biohazard decontamination is the safe removal, cleaning and disinfection of blood and other body fluids, and of the materials they have soaked into, after an injury, a death, an assault or a similar event. It is not ordinary cleaning. The hazards are biological (blood-borne viruses), physical (sharps, broken glass, structural damage), chemical (concentrated disinfectants) and psychological (what the crew sees and hears, and the grief around them). Every one of them is managed before the first bag is opened.

This course is the full credential course for the CARSI Trauma & Biohazard Decontamination Practitioner designation, a CARSI Southern Hemisphere Restoration Designation. It is produced for Australia and New Zealand. In Australia the model Work Health and Safety (WHS) laws apply in every jurisdiction except Victoria, which has its own Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004. In New Zealand the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 (HSWA) places the primary duty on the person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU) to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of its workers. Where the two countries differ, each lesson states the New Zealand position beside the Australian one.

Six modules follow the order of a real job: the work and your conduct on site; blood-borne viruses, hepatitis B vaccination and what to do after an exposure; risk assessment, the Safe Work Method Statement (SWMS) and personal protective equipment (PPE); containment, removal and the clean-then-disinfect sequence; sharps and clinical waste under each state’s environment protection rules; and finally psychological safety, verification and the job file. Each module ends with a check. A practical task and a final designation exam complete the credential.

Standards are referenced by name only. The course is aligned to the principles in ANSI/IICRC S540:2023. No standard text is reproduced here. Where a lesson describes practice that a standard also addresses, the wording is CARSI’s own and is being confirmed by the course SME against his licensed copy.

The course builds judgement. It is no substitute for your employer’s procedures, a product’s label and Safety Data Sheet (SDS), medical advice after an exposure, or the instructions of police, a coroner or a regulator.

See it

The roadmap shows the six modules in the order a job runs, and where the practical task and the final designation exam sit.

Do it in metric

Size the job before you quote it. In the Parramatta unit, the affected bedroom measures 3.2 m by 2.6 m, which is 8.32 m². Write the area on the first-attendance card, then note which surfaces are porous (carpet, mattress, upholstery) and which are not (vinyl, tiles, sealed timber). Area and material drive your crew size, your PPE count and the number of clinical-waste containers you bring. In the Christchurch café, the affected vinyl is about 1.5 m by 1.0 m, which is 1.5 m², and the bench top is 0.6 m by 1.8 m, which is 1.08 m².

Field download

The Trauma site first-attendance card walks the first ten minutes: confirm authority and release, size the area in square metres, list porous and non-porous surfaces, and note who is on site.

Check yourself

The Module 1 check asks which law applies where, what makes this work different from ordinary cleaning, and how the designation is earned. Each answer carries a practitioner “why”.

Takeaway

This is safety-critical, people-critical work. Know which law applies (WHS, Victorian OHS or NZ HSWA), size the job in metric, and treat everyone on site with care. Next lesson: discretion, dignity and conduct on a trauma site.

Sources for this lesson

  • ANSI Webstore, ANSI/IICRC S540-2023 listing (edition details only). Read 02/11/2026.
  • Safe Work Australia, Model WHS laws. Read 02/11/2026.
  • New Zealand Legislation, Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, section 36. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Discretion, dignity and conduct on a trauma site
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Practice wording and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

You pull up outside the Parramatta block. Two neighbours are on the stairwell and a family member is waiting at the door. What you do in the next five minutes is remembered for years: whether you suited up on the footpath, whether the van carried large signage, whether someone on your crew joked in the corridor. Discretion is not an extra. It is part of doing the job properly.

The idea

Confirm release and authority first. Decontamination starts only after police, and the coroner where one is involved, have released the scene, and only on the instruction of someone with authority over the property: the owner, the executor, the property manager or the insurer’s representative. Write who released the scene, who instructed you and when. The exact release process differs between states and between Australia and New Zealand, so follow the instruction you are given and ask if it is unclear.

Arrive with a low profile. Use a discreet vehicle where you can, park considerately, and put on PPE inside the property or out of public view. Keep conversation professional and quiet. Photographs are for the job record only, taken of surfaces, never of people.

Protect the people on site. Your duty is not only to your crew. In Australia the PCBU’s primary duty covers workers and others who may be affected by the work, such as visitors. In New Zealand the primary duty under HSWA also extends to other people put at risk by the work, such as customers, visitors and the public. On a trauma site that means family members, neighbours and the client. Set a cordon, keep the door closed, and never let a family member walk into a contaminated area unprotected.

Communicate with care. Speak plainly and kindly. Explain what you will do, roughly how long it will take and what will be removed. Do not describe what you found. Ask before moving or discarding personal items; set aside documents, photographs, jewellery and keepsakes for the family where they can be safely cleaned or bagged. If a family member wants to talk, listen briefly and stay professional; refer them to support services rather than counselling them yourself.

Treat the job as confidential. Do not post, discuss or identify the job outside the crew and the client. Your job file holds the facts; nothing else leaves the site.

See it

The flow shows the conduct steps from the kerb to the final handover.

Do it in metric

Set the cordon to fit the space. At the Parramatta unit you mark a clean set-up area of 1.8 m by 1.2 m inside the front door, which is 2.16 m², for donning PPE out of sight of the stairwell. You keep two walkways of about 1.0 m² each clear between the set-up area and the bedroom. Record the dimensions on the first-attendance card so the next crew sets up the same way.

Field download

The Trauma site first-attendance card carries the release-and-authority box, the low-profile arrival checklist and the personal-items log.

Check yourself

The module check asks when work may start, who your duty extends to, and how to handle personal items. Each answer explains the reason.

Takeaway

Confirm release and authority, arrive quietly, protect everyone on site, communicate plainly and keep the job confidential. Next module: the blood-borne viruses this work exposes you to, and how to protect yourself.

Sources for this lesson

  • Safe Work Australia, Duties of a PCBU. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe New Zealand, What is the primary duty of care?. Read 02/11/2026.

modules.title: Module 2: Blood-Borne Viruses and Protecting Yourself

lessons.title: Blood-borne viruses and how exposure happens
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Scenario and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

In the Christchurch café a dried stain runs along the kitchen floor and under the edge of the bench. A new crew member kneels to look closer, bare-handed, with a cut on his knuckle from the weekend. Nothing about the stain looks dangerous. That is the point: you cannot tell by looking whether blood carries a virus, so you treat all of it as if it does.

The idea

Blood-borne viruses spread when infected blood or other body fluids pass from one person to another. The major blood-borne viruses in Australia are hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV, and the same three matter in New Zealand. Each can cause serious long-term illness, and a person can carry one without knowing.

At work, exposure happens in three main ways. A sharps injury: a needle, broken glass or a sharp fragment breaks the skin. A splash into the eyes, nose or mouth: mucous membranes absorb what lands on them. Contact with non-intact skin: cuts, grazes, dermatitis or chapped hands let fluid in. Intact skin is a good barrier; broken skin is not. That is why the crew member’s cut knuckle matters more than the stain.

Keep the risk in proportion. The chance of infection from a needlestick injury is low, especially when workplace safety guidelines are followed. Low is not zero, and the consequences are severe, which is why the controls are strict and applied every time.

The controls are called standard precautions: people exposed to blood or body fluids should routinely follow them, whatever the source. In practice they mean handling and disposing of sharps safely, wearing gloves when handling body fluids, using goggles or face shields when splashes are likely, covering cuts with a waterproof dressing before gloving, keeping hands away from the face, and washing hands after removing gloves. You apply them to every job, because you rarely know the health status of the person whose blood it is, and you never ask the family.

Dried blood still counts. Scraping, scrubbing or pressure-washing can flick particles and droplets towards the face, so eye protection and the right respirator matter during removal, not only when fluid is wet.

See it

The diagram links the three viruses to the three exposure routes, and shows standard precautions as the barrier that blocks each route.

Do it in metric

Plan the work area around the stain, not only the stain. The visible stain on the café floor is 0.6 m by 0.4 m, which is 0.24 m². Add a 0.5 m clear margin on every side for kneeling and tools, and your work area becomes 1.6 m by 1.4 m, which is 2.24 m². Everyone inside that 2.24 m² wears gloves and eye protection; anyone outside it stays out until the area is cleaned.

Field download

The Blood and body fluid exposure response card lists the three exposure routes and the standard-precaution barrier for each.

Check yourself

The module check asks how blood-borne viruses spread, which exposure route the cut knuckle represents, and why standard precautions apply to every job.

Takeaway

Three viruses, three routes. Treat all blood as infectious, cover broken skin, protect the eyes, nose and mouth, and handle sharps as if each one carries a virus. Next lesson: hepatitis B vaccination and what to do after an exposure.

Sources for this lesson

  • healthdirect, Blood-borne viruses (BBVs). Read 02/11/2026.
  • Queensland Health, Management of occupational exposure to blood and body fluids. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Australian Immunisation Handbook, Hepatitis B. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Australian Immunisation Handbook, Vaccination for people at occupational risk. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Hepatitis B vaccination and the exposure response
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Timings and dates are illustrative and flagged for verification. This lesson is not medical advice.

On the job

On a Tuesday at 2:00 pm a technician lifting a mattress in Parramatta feels a sharp jab through his glove. He does not know what it was. His supervisor’s next ten minutes, and the decisions over the next three days, matter more than anything else on the job.

The idea

Vaccinate before the work. In Australia, the Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends hepatitis B vaccine for people whose work involves handling human tissue, blood or body fluids, or used needles or syringes, if they are not immune, and it names other workers with regular contact with human tissue, blood or body fluids among those recommended. The adult vaccine is a 3-dose schedule. People at significant occupational risk are recommended to have a blood test (serology) 4 to 8 weeks after finishing the course to confirm they responded. In New Zealand, the Immunisation Handbook lists hepatitis B vaccine as recommended, but not funded, for adults at increased risk from occupational exposure to body fluids, and notes that some people who need protection for their employment require post-vaccination serology. Talk to your GP; keep a copy of your vaccination and serology record in your personnel file.

First aid in the first minutes. For a needlestick or cut, wash the wound with soap and water for at least 30 seconds, then go straight to a doctor or the nearest hospital emergency department. Do not squeeze the wound to make it bleed. For a splash to the eyes, irrigate well with clean water or saline. For the mouth, spit and rinse with water. Remove contaminated clothing.

Report and get assessed the same day. Tell your supervisor straight away and record the time, the task and what happened. Medical assessment decides on testing and treatment. If HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is recommended, it should start as soon as possible and within 72 hours. There is no post-exposure prophylaxis for hepatitis C, which is why prevention matters so much. For a non-immune worker, the doctor will also consider hepatitis B protection; in New Zealand the Handbook lists hepatitis B vaccine as recommended and funded following a needle-stick injury.

Where to call. In an emergency call 000 in Australia or 111 in New Zealand. For health advice, healthdirect is on 1800 022 222 in Australia and Healthline is free on 0800 611 116 in New Zealand.

The supervisor’s job is to make this easy: stop the work, get the worker washed and to a doctor, record the incident, and check the support the worker needs afterwards. Exposures are frightening; a calm, practised response reduces the fear as well as the risk.

See it

The timeline runs left to right from the moment of exposure, with the Australian and New Zealand vaccination positions underneath.

Do it in metric

Work the clock. The jab happened at 2:00 pm Tuesday; the 72-hour PEP window closes at 2:00 pm Friday, but “as soon as possible” means today. The wash takes at least 30 seconds of running water, so a 10 L water container in the van gives you enough for several thorough washes on a site with no tap. For vaccination planning: a worker who finishes the 3-dose course on 1 March has serology between 29 March and 26 April (4 to 8 weeks).

Field download

The Blood and body fluid exposure response card is the wallet card: wash, report, get assessed, the 72-hour clock, and the AU and NZ numbers.

Check yourself

The module check asks for the first-aid steps, the PEP window, and the hepatitis B positions in Australia and New Zealand.

Takeaway

Get vaccinated and confirm immunity before the work. After an exposure: wash for 30 seconds, report, get assessed the same day, and remember the 72-hour window. Next module: risk assessment and the SWMS.

Sources for this lesson

  • Australian Immunisation Handbook, Hepatitis B. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Australian Immunisation Handbook, Vaccination for people at occupational risk. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Australian Immunisation Handbook, Serological testing 4 to 8 weeks after the hepatitis B vaccine course. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Health New Zealand, Immunisation Handbook, chapter 9: Hepatitis B. Read 02/11/2026.
  • healthdirect, Needlestick injuries. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Queensland Health, Management of occupational exposure to blood and body fluids. Read 02/11/2026.
  • ASHM, Australian National Guidelines for Post-Exposure Prophylaxis after Non-Occupational and Occupational Exposure to HIV (October 2025). Read 02/11/2026.
  • Healthdirect Australia, Need help now. Read 02/11/2026.

modules.title: Module 3: Risk Assessment, SWMS and PPE

lessons.title: Site risk assessment and the SWMS
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Scenario and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

Before anyone enters the Parramatta bedroom, the supervisor stands at the doorway with a torch and a clipboard. The room has been closed for several days in warm weather. There is a stained carpet, a mattress, a bedside table with medication packets, and a power board behind the bed. The supervisor’s first job is not cleaning. It is deciding how the crew will do this safely, and writing it down.

The idea

The duty. In Australia, a duty holder must manage risks by eliminating them so far as is reasonably practicable, and if that is not reasonably practicable, minimising them. Elimination is the best way to manage risk; administrative controls and PPE are the least effective. In Victoria the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 sets the same direction, aiming to eliminate risks at the source. In New Zealand the General Risk and Workplace Management Regulations 2016 set the hierarchy in law: if elimination is not reasonably practicable, substitute, isolate or engineer; then use administrative controls; and only if a risk then remains, provide and use suitable PPE. WorkSafe NZ is clear that PPE should not be the first or only control considered.

Applying it to a trauma site. Eliminate: remove the affected mattress whole, wrapped, rather than cutting it open in the room. Substitute: a less hazardous product that does the same job. Isolate: close the room, set zones and keep family out. Engineer: ventilation and HEPA-filtered extraction where dust or aerosols are made. Administrative: the SWMS, the zone rules, work-rest blocks and a buddy system. PPE: the last line, chosen for the hazards that remain.

What to look for. Biological: blood and body fluids, including where they have run under floor coverings, into furniture and behind skirting. Sharps: needles, glass, broken fittings. Chemical: concentrated disinfectants, medication, unknown substances. Electrical: power boards and leads near wet cleaning; all portable gear goes through a residual current device (safety switch), which in Australian workplaces must trip at no more than 30 mA for socket outlets up to 20 A, and leads are tested and tagged. In New Zealand, check WorkSafe NZ’s electrical guidance for the equivalent rule. Physical: lifting mattresses and furniture, slips, heat strain inside full PPE. Psychological: what the crew will see and smell (Module 6).

The SWMS. A Safe Work Method Statement records the task steps, the hazards at each step and the controls. Write it for this site, brief the crew on it before entry, and stop and revise it when something changes, such as finding sharps or a second affected room. If a hazard cannot be controlled, stop and escalate: to your supervisor, a licensed electrician, a licensed asbestos assessor if materials you must cut may contain asbestos (in Australia, assume asbestos may be present in any building built or renovated before 31 December 2003, when the national ban took effect, with buildings built or renovated before 1990 the most likely to contain it; in New Zealand, any building built or renovated before 2000 could contain asbestos), or 000 or 111 in an emergency.

See it

Read the ladder from the top: the higher the control, the more it protects without relying on people getting it right.

Do it in metric

Measure and power the job. The bedroom is 3.2 m by 2.6 m, which is 8.32 m². You need light, so you run two 230 V work lights drawing about 0.5 A each, 1.0 A in total, through a portable RCD from a 10 A GPO in the hallway, leaving plenty of headroom on that circuit. Record the area, the GPO used and the RCD test on the SWMS.

Field download

The Site risk assessment, SWMS and PPE sheet has the hazard walk, the control ladder with a box per rung, and a sign-on panel for the crew briefing.

Check yourself

The module check asks which control is strongest, where PPE sits in the AU and NZ hierarchy, and what to do when the site changes.

Takeaway

Assess before you enter. Work down the hierarchy, write the SWMS for this site, brief the crew, and stop when something changes. Next lesson: choosing, fitting and removing PPE.

Sources for this lesson

  • Safe Work Australia, Manage the risks. Read 02/11/2026.
  • New Zealand Legislation, Health and Safety at Work (General Risk and Workplace Management) Regulations 2016, regulation 6. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe New Zealand, Identifying, assessing and managing work risks. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe Victoria, Information for employers: Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe ACT, Residual current devices. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Selecting, fitting and removing PPE
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. The donning and doffing order and the figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

Halfway through the Parramatta job a technician steps out to answer his phone, pulls his mask down to talk, and walks back in with gloves he has been wearing for an hour. Every piece of PPE he had on was right. The way he used it undid all of it.

The idea

Select for the hazard that remains. After the higher controls, PPE protects against what is left: contact with blood and body fluids, splashes, and particles or droplets made during removal and scrubbing. A typical set is fluid-resistant disposable coveralls with a hood, disposable nitrile gloves (often double-gloved, the outer pair changed when torn or heavily soiled), boot covers or washable boots, eye protection or a face shield, and a respirator chosen for the task. Occupational protective gloves are covered by AS/NZS 2161.10.

Respirators, not surgical masks. A surgical mask protects against splashes of large droplets of blood or body fluids only; it does not protect against small particles or aerosols. When the work makes droplets or dust, use a respirator. Respirators used at work should comply with AS/NZS 1716. Particulate filters (P1, P2, P3) protect against solid and liquid particles including micro-organisms, but not against gases or vapours, so a disinfectant with strong vapour may need a combined filter per its SDS. Workers must pass a fit test before first wearing a tight-fitting respirator, and they fit-check it each time it goes on. Facial hair under the seal defeats it.

Who provides it. PPE is provided by the business. In Australia the model WHS Regulations say the PCBU must give workers PPE if they need it, and a worker does not pay for it; in New Zealand the PCBU who directs the work must provide PPE to the workers carrying it out (GRWM Regulations 2016, regulation 15), and must make sure it fits, is maintained and is worn.

Put it on in the clean zone. Hand hygiene; coveralls; boot covers; respirator and fit check; eye protection; hood up; inner gloves; outer gloves over the cuffs, taped if your procedure says so.

Take it off in the transition zone, dirtiest first. Outer gloves; coverall rolled outwards and down, touching the inside only; boot covers; inner gloves; then hand hygiene; then eye protection and respirator by the straps; hand hygiene again. Bag everything as clinical waste. Never touch your face, phone or keys in between.

Heat. Full PPE traps heat. Plan work blocks with breaks out of PPE, drink water, and watch each other for signs of heat strain.

See it

Left column: putting PPE on. Right column: taking it off, dirtiest item first, hands last.

Do it in metric

Count the PPE before you leave the depot. Two technicians each work three 45-minute blocks, changing into a fresh coverall each block: that is 6 coveralls. Double gloving with a fresh pair of each per block means at least 12 pairs of gloves, plus spares for tears. Pack respirator filters, 2 face shields and a 10 L water container for hand washing and drinking.

Field download

The Site risk assessment, SWMS and PPE sheet lists the PPE set, the donning and doffing order, and a fit-test record line for each worker.

Check yourself

The module check asks why a surgical mask is not enough, what must happen before a tight-fitting respirator is first worn, and which item comes off first.

Takeaway

PPE is the last line, so choose it for the hazards that remain, fit-test respirators, and take it off dirtiest first with hand hygiene between steps. Next module: containment and removal.

Sources for this lesson

  • WorkSafe Queensland, Respiratory protective equipment (RPE). Read 02/11/2026.
  • SafeWork SA, Fit testing and fit checking of RPE. Read 02/11/2026.
  • New Zealand Legislation, Health and Safety at Work (General Risk and Workplace Management) Regulations 2016, regulations 15 to 19. Read 02/11/2026.
  • NSW Health, Clinical and Related Waste Management for Health Services (PD2020_049). Read 02/11/2026.
  • Safe Work Australia, Personal protective equipment (PPE): overview. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Zones, containment and removing affected materials
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Zone layout, the cut-out margin and the figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

The carpet in the Parramatta bedroom shows a stain about 1.2 m by 0.9 m. Peel the edge back and the underlay is stained further out, and there is a mark on the concrete beneath. What you can see on the surface is rarely the full extent. Containment and removal is about finding the real edge and getting it out without spreading it.

The idea

Set three zones. A contaminated zone around the affected area, where full PPE is worn. A transition zone at its edge, where waste is bagged and sealed, tools are wiped down and PPE comes off. A clean zone near the entry for donning, equipment and paperwork. People and equipment move clean to dirty on the way in, and come out only through the transition zone. Mark the zones with tape or signs and keep doors closed. Protect the path between zones with disposable floor protection where you will carry waste.

Find the real extent. Blood and body fluids migrate: under carpet into underlay and onto the slab or boards, between floorboards, into mattress and upholstery foam, behind skirting, under appliances and into gaps. Inspect beyond the visible edge. A working rule many crews use is to cut carpet and underlay at least 300 mm past the visible stain and check the floor beneath before deciding the boundary.

Decide: remove or clean. Porous materials saturated with blood, such as carpet, underlay, mattresses and upholstery foam, are usually removed and disposed of as clinical waste, because they cannot be reliably cleaned through. Non-porous surfaces, such as tiles, vinyl, glass, metal and sealed timber, are usually cleaned and disinfected in place. Semi-porous items, such as unsealed timber or grout, need judgement and may need sealing or replacement. Record each call, with the reason and a photograph. In New South Wales, waste containing visibly blood-stained body fluids, materials or equipment is clinical waste, which is why removed material goes to the clinical waste stream (Module 5), not the skip.

Remove without spreading. Remove gross material first with disposable tools. Wrap and seal large items such as mattresses in heavy plastic in the room before carrying them out. Cut carpet into manageable rolls, folded contaminated face inwards. Avoid dry brushing, which disperses particles; mist and wipe instead. Keep extraction or air movement from blowing across the affected area towards the clean zone. In Victoria and other jurisdictions, check your state environment protection rules for how removed material must be packaged and carried; Module 5 covers New South Wales, Victoria and New Zealand.

See it

The plan shows the three zones and the direction people, equipment and waste move.

Do it in metric

Work out the cut. The visible stain is 1.2 m by 0.9 m. Add 300 mm on each side and the cut-out becomes 1.8 m by 1.5 m, which is 2.7 m² of carpet and underlay to remove. Record 2.7 m² on the removal log with photographs before and after, and note that the slab beneath measured the same 1.8 m by 1.5 m for cleaning.

Field download

The Zones, removal and disinfection log has a zone sketch grid, a remove-or-clean decision table with reasons, and the area removed in square metres.

Check yourself

The module check asks which zone PPE comes off in, why the visible stain is not the boundary, and which materials are usually removed.

Takeaway

Zone the site, find the real extent, decide remove or clean with a reason, and get material out without spreading it. Next lesson: cleaning, then disinfecting.

Sources for this lesson

  • NSW EPA, Waste classification guidelines Part 1: Classifying waste. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Clean, then disinfect: products, claims and contact time
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Label rates, contact times and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification. Always follow the product label and SDS.

On the job

On the Christchurch café bench a crew member sprays disinfectant straight onto a dried stain, wipes it after ten seconds and moves on. The surface looks clean. It has not been disinfected: the soil shielded what was underneath, and the product never stayed wet long enough to work.

The idea

Clean first. Thorough cleaning must be completed before disinfection, or be built into a two-in-one product used exactly as its label directs. Dirt and grime stop effective disinfection by preventing surface contact or affecting how well the disinfectant works. So: remove gross soil with disposable tools, clean with detergent and water, then disinfect. Clean from high to low and from clean to dirty, so you do not drag soil across finished surfaces.

Use the label, all of it. Make up the product at the label rate, with measured water, not by eye. Apply it so the surface stays visibly wet for the full contact time stated on the label, then wipe or rinse as directed. A disinfectant may have a minimum contact time for which it must stay wet to be effective. Read the SDS for the PPE and ventilation it needs, and never mix cleaning products: harmful chemical reactions can occur.

Check the claim: Australia. The Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) regulates disinfectants by what they claim. A claim that a product kills, or is active against, viruses, spores, tuberculosis, mycobacteria or fungi is a “specific claim”, and disinfectants that make these claims require listing on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG) before supply. Hard-surface disinfectants that make no specific claims are exempt from ARTG inclusion but still have to meet the TGA requirements. If you will rely on a product’s activity against blood-borne viruses, check that it makes that claim and look up its ARTG entry, and record the product name and ARTG number in the job file.

Check the claim: New Zealand. In New Zealand, disinfectants are hazardous substances. The Environmental Protection Authority (EPA NZ) approves and classifies hazardous substances, and WorkSafe NZ enforces the workplace rules. The EPA’s Cleaning Products (Subsidiary Hazard) Group Standard 2020 lists antimicrobial products among the typical substances it covers, and disinfectants sold for home use carry a hazard label. Before relying on a kill claim in New Zealand, check with EPA NZ and ask the supplier for the test evidence behind the claim; keep the label, SDS and evidence in the job file.

Porous contents. Soft furnishings and personal items that can be cleaned are handled to the same rule: clean, then disinfect only with a product labelled for that material, and test an inconspicuous spot first.

See it

The steps run left to right; the claim checks underneath are what you confirm before you choose the product.

Do it in metric

Mix by measure. The label (illustrative here) directs 20 mL of concentrate per litre of water. Your bucket holds 5 L, so you add 100 mL of concentrate, measured in a graduated jug. The label contact time is 10 minutes. The café floor and bench total about 2.6 m², and the slab in Parramatta is 2.7 m², so you work each in sections small enough to keep wet for the full 10 minutes, re-wetting if a section starts to dry.

Field download

The Zones, removal and disinfection log records each product, its ARTG number or NZ label and SDS, the dilution, the area treated in m² and the contact time achieved.

Check yourself

The module check asks why cleaning comes first, what a “specific claim” is in Australia, and what you check in New Zealand.

Takeaway

Clean, then disinfect. Measure the dilution, keep it wet for the contact time, never mix products, and check the claim: ARTG in Australia, EPA NZ label and supplier evidence in New Zealand. Next module: sharps and clinical waste.

lessons.title: Sharps: find, handle and contain
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Search technique and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

A technician in Parramatta runs his gloved hand along the gap between the mattress and the bed base to free a sheet. Gloves stop fluid; they do not stop a needle. Sharps injuries on trauma sites happen in exactly these places: bedding, pockets, gaps in furniture, bins and under rugs.

The idea

Look, do not feel. Before you lift, fold or reach into anything, look. Use good light and a torch. Move bedding, cushions and clothing with tongs or a probe, not hands. Never reach blind into gaps, pockets or bags. Empty bins by tipping them gently onto a tray, not by reaching in. Wear puncture-resistant gloves over your nitrile gloves where your procedure requires them for searching.

Handle with tools, one at a time. Pick up each sharp with tongs, point away from you. Never recap a needle, bend it or break it. Carry the sharps container to the sharp, not the sharp to the container, and place it on a stable surface beside you.

Use a proper container. Sharps go into a rigid, puncture-resistant sharps container, never into a waste bag. AS/NZS 23907:2023 replaced the older AS 4031 and AS/NZS 4261 container standards, and it was approved for New Zealand on 1 October 2025. Regulators that reference the standard may apply it on their own timeline, so check which edition your state or council rules name; WorkSafe ACT, for example, still refers to bins meeting AS 4031 and AS 4261. Whatever the edition, used sharps and infectious waste cannot go into general rubbish or recycling at a workplace.

Fill to the line, then close. Never overfill. Stop at the fill line marked on the container, engage the permanent closure, and label it for the clinical waste stream with your business name. A closed container is never reopened.

Other sharps. Broken glass, mirror, razor blades and sharp fragments are handled the same way: tools, not hands, and a rigid container. Medication found on site is set aside for the client or police, as instructed, not thrown out.

If an injury happens, follow the exposure response from Module 2: wash for at least 30 seconds, report, get assessed the same day. For a chemical splash, call the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 in Australia or the National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766 in New Zealand, and 000 or 111 if the person is unconscious or has difficulty breathing.

See it

The steps run from searching to closing the container, with the rules that apply at every step.

Do it in metric

Size the container to the job. A 5 L container with a fill line at about three-quarters holds roughly 3.75 L of sharps before it must be closed. On a site where you expect several needles and broken glass, take two 5 L containers so you never push one past its line.

Field download

The Sharps and clinical waste checklist has the search pattern, the never-do list and the container label panel.

Check yourself

The module check asks where sharps never go, which way the container moves, and when a container is closed.

Takeaway

Look before you touch, use tools, carry the container to the sharp, stop at the fill line, and never put a sharp in a bag. Next lesson: packaging, labelling and disposing of clinical waste.

lessons.title: Clinical waste: package, label, track and dispose
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Bag sizes and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification. Check your own state EPA or NZ council rules.

On the job

At the end of the Parramatta job there are three bags of carpet and underlay, a wrapped mattress, and a closed sharps container in the transition zone. The client asks if you can “just put it in the skip”. You cannot, and you need to be able to explain why.

The idea

It is regulated waste. Material contaminated with blood is clinical waste. In New South Wales, clinical and related waste is pre-classified as “special waste”, and the definition includes waste containing visibly blood-stained materials. Each state and territory environment protection authority (EPA) sets its own rules, so the operator confirms the rule where the job is. This lesson uses New South Wales and Victoria as worked examples and gives the New Zealand position.

Package and label. Non-sharps clinical waste goes into a rigid-walled container or a bag that is labelled to AS/NZS 3816; the NSW Waste Regulation names the 1998 edition, while NSW Health policy lists AS/NZS 3816:2018, so check which your contractor and regulator apply. Do not fill waste bags beyond two-thirds of their capacity, so they can be closed securely without compaction. Sharps never go in waste bags. Close bags at the transition zone, wipe the outside if soiled, and place them in the contractor’s rigid bin.

New South Wales: transport and tracking. In NSW clinical waste in transport is carried in rigid, leak-proof, lidded containers, and not in a vehicle with a compaction system. The transport and disposal of hazardous waste listed in Schedule 1 of the Waste Regulation must be tracked, with authorisation and documents that follow each load. Use a licensed clinical waste contractor and keep the paperwork.

Victoria: permits and Waste Tracker. In Victoria, clinical and related wastes (waste code R100) are reportable priority waste. Transporting them needs a high-risk transport permit, and each change of hands is recorded in EPA Victoria’s Waste Tracker. Waste may only go to a place authorised to receive it. The permit and tracking requirements fall away only for a net load under 50 litres carried for no fee or reward, which a paid decontamination job never is.

New Zealand. NZS 4304:2002 Management of Healthcare Waste sets out classification, segregation, packaging, labelling, storage, transport and disposal of healthcare waste, and each regional and local authority has its own plans controlling waste treatment and disposal. Council trade waste bylaws reference NZS 4304 for what may not be discharged to the wastewater network, so never pour contaminated rinse water down a drain without checking the local rule. Use a licensed healthcare waste contractor and confirm the council requirements for the district.

Other jurisdictions. Queensland, Western Australia, South Australia, Tasmania, the Northern Territory and the ACT each set their own clinical waste rules. Check with your EPA and your contractor before the job, not after.

See it

The chain runs left to right; each jurisdiction box shows the rule that applies at that link.

Do it in metric

Do the volume sum. Each 72 L bag filled to two-thirds holds 48 L. Three bags make 144 L, before the mattress and the sharps container. That is nearly three times the Victorian 50 L figure, and the job is paid, so in Victoria the load needs a permitted transporter and a Waste Tracker record. Book the contractor bins by volume: list the bags, the mattress dimensions (for example 1.9 m by 1.4 m) and each 5 L sharps container.

Field download

The Sharps and clinical waste checklist has the packaging rules, a volume calculator, and the NSW, Victorian and NZ paperwork boxes to fill.

Check yourself

The module check asks how full a waste bag may be, what Victoria requires for a paid load, and which NZ standard covers healthcare waste.

Takeaway

Clinical waste is regulated waste. Package and label it properly, fill bags no more than two-thirds, use a licensed contractor, keep the tracking records, and check your state EPA or NZ council. Next module: looking after your crew, verification and the job file.

modules.title: Module 6: Psychological Safety, Verification and the Job File

lessons.title: Psychosocial hazards and looking after your crew
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Crew practices and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification. This lesson is not clinical advice.

On the job

Three weeks after a difficult job, an experienced technician starts calling in sick on Mondays and snaps at the apprentice. Nobody connects it to the job. The hazard on a trauma site is not only what can be cut, splashed or breathed. It is what the crew sees, smells and carries home.

The idea

It is a workplace hazard, in law. In Australia, health under the model WHS Act means both physical and psychological health, and the model WHS Regulations set specific duties to manage psychosocial risks in Part 3.1 and Part 3.2, Division 11. The model regulations and Code apply in a jurisdiction only once it implements them, so check your regulator. Safe Work Australia names exposure to traumatic events or materials as a psychosocial hazard. In Victoria, the Occupational Health and Safety (Psychological Health) Regulations 2025 commenced on 1 December 2025, and name exposure to traumatic events or content among the psychosocial hazards employers must address. In New Zealand, HSWA defines health as physical and mental health, and WorkSafe NZ says businesses must manage psychosocial risks at work, weighing how often, how long and how intensely workers are exposed.

Before the job. Tell people when they apply what the job involves, including possible exposure to trauma. Brief the crew before entry on what they are likely to see and smell, without graphic detail, and let anyone step back without penalty.

During the job. Minimise the number of traumatic jobs each worker does, for example by rotating people through different roles. Increase breaks, recovery time and support when workers are exposed. Use a buddy system and short check-ins. Give people a clean space away from the affected room to take a break out of PPE.

After the job. A short, practical end-of-job debrief: what went well, what was hard, what we change next time. Check in again over the following days. Know the signs that someone is struggling: sleep problems, withdrawal, irritability, drinking more, avoiding certain jobs. Make support easy to reach through an employee assistance program if you have one, a GP, or a support line.

Support lines. Australia: Lifeline 13 11 14 and Beyond Blue 1300 22 4636, and 000 in an emergency. New Zealand: call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor, and 111 in an emergency. Supervisors are not counsellors; their job is to notice, ask, and connect people to help.

The family. Families are grieving. Be kind and brief, and refer them to the same support lines rather than taking on that role yourself.

See it

The diagram groups the controls by when they happen, with the law and the support numbers along the bottom.

Do it in metric

Plan exposure, not only area. The Parramatta job has about 14 m² of affected surfaces across the bedroom and hallway. At roughly 3.5 m² per 45-minute block, that is four blocks. With two technicians alternating, each works two blocks in the affected room, with a 15-minute break out of PPE between blocks, and the second technician handles waste and set-up while the first works.

Field download

The Crew wellbeing and handover checklist has the pre-job brief prompts, the rotation and break plan, the end-of-job debrief questions and the AU and NZ support numbers.

Check yourself

The module check asks which law covers psychological health in each country, one control for each stage of the job, and the support numbers.

Takeaway

Traumatic exposure is a recognised psychosocial hazard in Australia and New Zealand. Brief honestly, limit and rotate exposure, build in breaks, debrief and follow up. Next lesson: verification, handover and the job file.

lessons.title: Verification, handover and the defensible job file
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Handover criteria and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

Two months after the Parramatta job, the property manager emails: a new tenant says there is a mark under the bed. Your answer depends entirely on what is in your job file. If it shows the area, what was removed, what was cleaned with which product and for how long, the photographs and a signed handover, you can respond calmly. If it does not, you are guessing.

The idea

Verify before you hand over. Before the crew leaves, the supervisor walks the site in clean PPE with good light. Check that no visible residue remains on any surface in or near the affected area, that every porous item marked for removal has gone, that cleaned surfaces have had the full contact time, that no odour source remains, and that the floor beneath any removed covering has been treated. Walk the client or their representative through the result, and record their sign-off. If something fails, fix it and check again.

Build the job file as you go. Contemporaneous records are your evidence. The file holds: who instructed you and who released the scene, with dates and times; the SWMS and the crew briefing sign-on; the fit-test and vaccination confirmations for each worker; the zone sketch; the remove-or-clean decisions with reasons and photographs; each product, its ARTG number or NZ label and SDS, dilution, area and contact time; the sharps and clinical waste record, including the contractor, the tracking documents and, in Victoria, the Waste Tracker record (the waste producer keeps a copy); any incident or exposure and the response; and the handover walk-through and sign-off.

Photographs, with respect. Take photographs of surfaces and materials for the record only, before and after. Do not photograph people or personal items beyond what the file needs, and never share job images outside the job.

Your duties stay yours. In Australia a duty holder cannot transfer their WHS duties to another person: a client’s instruction to “skip the paperwork” or a subcontract does not move your safety duty. The same principle runs through NZ HSWA. Write the file so a stranger could reconstruct the job from it.

Hand back the property. Return keys, set aside personal items in sealed, labelled bags for the family, remove all zone tape and floor protection, and leave a short written summary of what was done and anything the client still needs to arrange, such as replacing removed carpet.

See it

Each box is a record that is made at the time the work happens, not written up afterwards.

Do it in metric

Write the numbers in. The Parramatta file reads: bedroom 8.32 m²; carpet and underlay removed 2.7 m²; slab cleaned and disinfected 2.7 m² at 20 mL per litre, 10 minutes wet; three 72 L clinical waste bags at 48 L each and one wrapped mattress; one 5 L sharps container closed at the fill line; handover walk-through at 4:30 pm and client sign-off.

Field download

The Crew wellbeing and handover checklist closes with the verification walk-through, the job-file contents list and the sign-off panel.

Check yourself

The module check asks what the handover check confirms, what goes in the job file and whether a client can take over your duty. The final designation exam follows.

Takeaway

Verify with good light before handover, build the job file as the work happens, photograph surfaces not people, and remember your duties cannot be handed to anyone else. Complete the practical task and the final exam to earn the designation.

Sources for this lesson

  • EPA Victoria, Waste Tracker. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Safe Work Australia, Principles that apply to work health and safety duties. Read 02/11/2026.
  • New Zealand Legislation, Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 (contents). Read 02/11/2026.
